Neonatal Mongolian gerbils emerge from the birth canal weighing just 3 grams [Wwb = 3 grams], a remarkably modest mass for an altricial rodent that underscores the extreme developmental immaturity characteristic of meriones neonates. These newborn pups, born after a relatively brief gestation period, are entirely dependent on maternal care and thermoregulation provided by the huddle within the nest. The species' core body temperature is tightly regulated at 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] which serves as the physiological baseline against which all developmental and reproductive metrics are evaluated in laboratory studies. Under these stable thermal conditions, parturition itself concludes a gestation that lasts 25 days [tg = 25 days], a duration that is typical for small-bodied murid rodents and reflects the accelerated pace of in utero organogenesis at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. The rapid onset of lactation immediately following delivery ensures that the pups receive colostrum and milk to fuel their swift postnatal growth trajectory.

Suckling juveniles progress through a well-defined developmental schedule that culminates in nutritional independence. At the species' normal body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], weaning occurs at 24 days after birth [tx = 24 days after birth] representing the point at which the young transition entirely from maternal milk to solid food items such as seeds and grains. At this juncture, a typical weanling weighs approximately 14.3 grams [Wwx = approximately 14.3 grams], reflecting a roughly fivefold increase over the birth mass achieved through efficient milk conversion and the onset of independent foraging behaviors. The timing of weaning in Meriones unguiculatus is relatively early compared to some other gerbil species, a life-history trait that may be linked to the high reproductive potential of females and the need to rapidly prepare the mother for successive litters. This developmental milestone marks a critical transition in the pup's life from a nutritionally subsidized existence to one requiring active food acquisition.

Sexual maturation in the Mongolian gerbil follows a sexually dimorphic schedule that is of considerable interest to comparative reproductive physiologists. At the core body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], the time since birth at puberty in females is documented as 43 days [tp = 43 days], a notably rapid attainment of reproductive capability that enables early breeding within the natal season. Males, in contrast, exhibit a slightly accelerated trajectory, achieving puberty at 36 days after birth [tp = 36 days after birth] under identical thermal conditions at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This earlier maturation of males relative to females is common among polygynous rodent species, where early testicular descent and spermatogenesis confer a competitive advantage in securing mating opportunities. The onset of gonadal activity is accompanied by a suite of behavioral changes, including scent-marking and territorial aggression, particularly in males. The post-weaning growth phase linking a weanling mass of 14.3 grams to adult dimensions represents a period of rapid somatic development fueled by high food intake.

Reproductive output in the Mongolian gerbil is characterized by a high intrinsic capacity for population increase, a trait consistent with the species' evolutionary history as a colonizer of arid steppe environments. Under optimal husbandry at the typical body temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], females produce litters containing 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter], and they achieve approximately 4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 litters per year]. This combination of moderate litter size and high iteroparity enables a substantial annual reproductive output. The postpartum estrus in this species allows females to become gravid again within hours of parturition, contributing to the achievement of these high litter frequencies. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult is 53.2 grams [Wwi = 53.2 grams], a value that positions Meriones unguiculatus among the medium-sized members of the genus Meriones. This adult mass is roughly seventeen times greater than the 3 gram birth mass indicating the substantial scope for postnatal somatic growth.

Longevity records for the Mongolian gerbil kept under standard vivarium conditions indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2300 days [am = approximately 2300 days], when maintained at a stable core temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This translates to about 6.3 years of life, a relatively extended lifespan for a rodent of this body size, which is likely related to the species' adaptation to unpredictable desert environments where delayed reproduction and bet-hedging life-history strategies may be favored. The long lifespan permits females to accumulate multiple breeding seasons over their lifetime, capitalizing on their ability to produce 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter] and 4 litters per year [F_R_i = 4 litters per year]. This reproductive strategy, characterized by moderate litter sizes but high iteroparity across an extended lifespan, represents a distinctive life-history syndrome among small desert rodents. The oldest recorded individuals exhibit signs of physiological senescence, including reduced fertility and diminished body condition, before natural death intervenes.
